Featured Startup Entrepreneurship Founders Product Strategy Startup Lessons The 7-Part Test I Run on a Startup Idea Before Anyone Writes Code Jev - CTO of techlead.fit 5 min read · Sep 27, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Try to answer questions or just try our AI startup check tool I automated it and ran 50 startups through it in two weeks. The same seven checks separated the ready from the not-ready every time. I build software for founders for a living, which means I spend a lot of time being the person who says “not yet.” Not because the ideas are bad. Because the founder is about to spend real money building something they have not pressure-tested, and once developers start, every gap they skipped comes back as a change request billed at build rates. Thinking and real life testing is cheap. Rework is not. For years I ran the same mental checklist on every idea that crossed my desk. Two weeks ago I turned it into a tool and let founders run it themselves: 18 questions across seven areas and structured report at the end. In those two weeks it evaluated more than 50 startups, with scores from 32 to 83 out of 100. Reading every report back, one thing became obvious. The strong ideas were strong in different ways. The weak ones failed the same seven checks, in the same order. Here is the test, and the exact failure signal each area kept surfacing, so you can run it on your own idea tonight. 1. Idea: is it a company or a feature? The failure signal: the idea only makes sense as an add-on to something that already exists. If your “startup” is a better notifications panel or a smarter export button, you have a feature. Features do not get funded, acquired, or defended. Ask whether anyone would switch to you for this alone. If the honest answer is no, you are building a roadmap item, not a business. 2. Problem: is it confirmed or assumed? The single most common weakness across all 50. Founders could describe their solution in exhausting detail and their problem in one borrowed sentence. Belief is not evidence. You believing the problem is real is the starting condition, not proof. The fix is uncomfortable and cheap: go find five people who have this problem and are not your friends, and confirm they have tried to solve it and paid for something already. If nobody has ever spent money or effort on it, it is an annoyance, not a problem. 3. Market: who exactly, and can you reach them? Weak reports had one word here: “everyone.” Small businesses. Busy professionals. People like me. A market you cannot name in one specific sentence is a market you cannot sell to. The test: name the first 100 customers concretely enough that you could list where they gather. If you cannot, your total addressable market is theoretical and your reachable market might be zero. 4. Go-to-market: a channel, or a hope? “Content and some ads” is not a plan. It is a hope with a budget attached, and it was the second-weakest area across the board. A real answer names one specific channel, why those people are already there, and why they would pay attention to you before your runway ends. If you cannot describe your first channel in a sentence that a stranger would find plausible, you have found your biggest unpriced risk. 5. Scope: can you name version one? The weak pattern: version one was also the final vision. Everything, for everyone, at launch. This is how six-week builds become six-month builds. The discipline is subtraction. Name the smallest version that delivers the core value to one type of user, and be able to defend why that version first. If every feature feels essential, you have not made a single real decision yet. 6. Execution: can this team, this budget, this timeline actually ship it? Here is the one founders skip entirely, and the one I care about most as a CTO. When the tool asked “why are you the right team to build this,” the weak answers were startlingly thin. No domain experience, no unfair access, no prior builds, no reason it should be them. Founder-market fit is not a soft factor. If you have no edge in the market you are entering, a better-positioned team will beat you to it. The fix before you write code: find a co-founder or first hire who closes that gap. 7. Vision: is there a believable path from small to large? The last check, and the one that separates a lifestyle project from a venture. A strong version one has to open a door to something bigger. Weak reports had a nice first product and no second act. Ask what the tenth product decision looks like if this works. If the ceiling is low, that is fine, but build accordingly and do not raise money against a ceiling you can already see. How to read your own result Run all seven and you will notice the same thing I did across 50 startups: almost nobody is even. A founder scoring 83 was usually excellent in four areas and way weaker in three. One scoring 40 was strong in one place and had never touched the rest. The single number hides the story. The spread is the story, because the seven are separate bets and they fail independently. You cannot average your way out of a zero in go-to-market with a brilliant product.
